Chapter 6


When Mrs. Wilkins woke up the next morning, she stayed in bed for a few minutes before getting up to open the shutters. What would she see outside her window? A sunny, bright world, or a rainy one? Either way, she knew it would be beautiful. Whatever the weather was, it would be wonderful.

She was in a small bedroom with plain white walls, a stone floor, and just a few pieces of old furniture. There were two black-enameled iron beds, decorated with painted bunches of bright flowers. She lay there, delaying the exciting moment of looking out the window, just like someone delays opening a special letter to enjoy the anticipation. She had no idea what time it was; she had forgotten to wind her watch ever since she last went to bed in Hampstead, which felt like centuries ago. The house was completely quiet, so she figured it must be very early, though she felt like she had slept for ages—she was completely rested and perfectly content.

She lay with her arms wrapped around her head, thinking about how happy she was, a delighted smile on her face. Being in bed by herself was absolutely wonderful. She hadn't slept in a bed without Mellersh for five whole years. The cool, spacious feel of it, the freedom to move around, the sheer thrill of pulling the blankets whenever she wanted, or adjusting the pillows to be more comfortable! It felt like discovering a completely new kind of joy.

Mrs. Wilkins wanted to get up and open the shutters, but staying in bed was just so delicious. She sighed with contentment and kept lying there, looking around her room. It was her own little room, hers to arrange exactly how she liked for this one blessed month. It was a room paid for with her own savings, the result of her careful budgeting and sacrifices. She could lock the door if she wanted to, and no one had the right to enter. It was a strange little room, very different from any she had lived in before, and so sweet. It felt like a monk's cell, but a happy one, except for having two beds.
she thought, quoting a favorite line and smiling at her surroundings,

Staying in bed and thinking about her happiness was wonderful, but she knew that whatever was outside the shutters would be even better. She jumped up, slipped on her slippers (since the stone floor only had one small rug), ran to the window, and threw open the shutters.

cried Mrs. Wilkins.

All the brightness of an Italian April lay spread out right in front of her. The sunshine poured over her, and the calm sea looked as if it were sleeping. Across the bay, the beautiful mountains, showing delicate shades of different colors, seemed to be sleeping in the light as well. Just beneath her window, at the bottom of a grassy slope covered in wildflowers where the castle wall stood, was a tall cypress tree. It stood out against the soft blues, purples, and pinks of the mountains and sea like a giant black sword.

She stared. There was so much beauty, and she was actually there to see it, alive to feel it. The sunlight bathed her face. Sweet scents rose up to the window, gently brushing against her. A soft breeze lifted her hair. Far out in the bay, a group of nearly still fishing boats looked like a flock of white birds resting on the quiet sea. It was incredibly beautiful. She was so grateful she hadn't died before seeing, breathing, and feeling this. She stared with her mouth slightly open. Was she happy?

was such a plain, ordinary word. How could she describe this feeling? It felt as if she couldn't contain herself, as if she were too small to hold so much joy, and as if she were completely bathed in light. It was amazing to feel such pure bliss when she wasn't doing—and didn't plan to do—a single unselfish thing, or anything she didn't want to do. According to everyone she had ever met, she should at least feel a little guilty. But she didn't feel guilty at all. Something seemed backward. It was strange that at home she had been so good, so incredibly good, yet had only felt miserable. There, she had dealt with all kinds of painful feelings, hurts, and disappointments, even though she was always being unselfish. Now she had taken off her goodness and left it behind like a pile of wet clothes in the rain, and she felt only joy. She was free of her past goodness, and she was happy to be free. She felt completely stripped of it and was celebrating. Meanwhile, back in the gloomy, damp air of Hampstead, Mellersh was probably being angry.

She tried to picture Mellersh having breakfast and thinking bitter thoughts about her. But as she tried, Mellersh's image began to shimmer, turning into pink, then soft violet, then a beautiful blue, before losing its shape and turning into glowing colors. After trembling for a moment, Mellersh completely dissolved into the light.

Mrs. Wilkins thought, staring at where his image had been. It was strange that she couldn't picture Mellersh, when she used to know every detail of his face and expression by heart. She simply couldn't see him as he normally looked. She could only see him blending into the beauty and harmony of her surroundings. The familiar words of the church's Thanksgiving prayer came naturally to her mind. She found herself thanking God out loud for creating her, keeping her safe, and giving her all the blessings of life—especially His great love. Meanwhile, at that exact moment, Mellersh was angrily pulling on his boots to go out into the rainy streets, thinking very bitter things about her.

She began to dress, choosing clean white clothes to suit the summery day, unpacking her bags, and tidying up her lovely room. She moved around quickly and with purpose, standing up straight, her small face—which had been wrinkled with stress and worry at home—now completely relaxed. Everything she had been and done before this morning, all her feelings and worries, had vanished. Each of her worries behaved just like Mellersh's image, dissolving into color and light. She even noticed things she hadn't paid attention to in years. While brushing her hair in front of the mirror, she looked at it and thought,

For years she had barely thought about it, braiding it at night and unbraiding it in the morning as quickly and carelessly as she tied her shoes. Now she actually saw it, wrapping it around her fingers in front of the mirror, glad that it was so nice. Mellersh must not have noticed it either, since he had never said anything about it. Well, when she got back home, she would make sure he noticed.
"look at my hair. Aren't you glad you have a wife with hair like curly honey?"

She laughed. She had never said anything like that to Mellersh, and the thought of it made her smile. But why hadn't she? Oh, right—she used to be afraid of him. It seemed silly now to be afraid of anyone, especially your own husband, whom you saw at his most vulnerable moments, like when he was fast asleep and snoring.

Once she was ready, she opened her door to check if Rose, who had been placed in the room opposite hers by a sleepy maid the night before, was awake. She would say good morning to her, then run down to spend some time by the cypress tree before breakfast. After breakfast, she wouldn't even look out the window until she had helped Rose prepare everything for Lady Caroline and Mrs. Fisher. There was a lot to do that day with unpacking and arranging the rooms, and she didn't want to leave Rose to do it all by herself. They would make everything beautiful for the other two women, preparing lovely, flower-filled rooms for them. She remembered that she hadn't wanted Lady Caroline to come. Imagine wanting to keep someone out of paradise just because she thought she would feel shy around her! As if it even mattered, and as if Lady Caroline would be shy anyway. Besides, it was a silly reason. She certainly couldn't call herself

for thinking that. She also remembered not wanting Mrs. Fisher to come because she seemed snobbish. It was so funny how she used to worry about such trivial things and make them seem important.

The bedrooms and two of the sitting rooms at San Salvatore were on the top floor, opening into a spacious hall with a large glass window at the north end. San Salvatore had many small gardens scattered in different areas and levels. The garden beneath this window was built on the highest part of the castle walls and could only be reached from a matching hall on the floor below. When Mrs. Wilkins walked out of her room, this window was wide open, and outside in the sunshine was a Judas tree in full bloom. There was no sign of anyone, and no sound of voices or footsteps. Tubs of lilies stood on the stone floor, and a large, bright bunch of nasturtiums sat on a table. The hall felt spacious, flowery, and quiet, with the open window leading to the garden and the beautiful Judas tree shining in the sun. Mrs. Wilkins, stopping on her way to see Mrs. Arbuthnot, felt it was too good to be true. Was she really going to live here for a whole month? Until now, she had only experienced beauty in small, snatched moments—a patch of daisies on a sunny day in Hampstead, or a glimpse of the sunset between chimney pots. She had never lived in a truly beautiful place or even in an old, historic house. Having lots of flowers in her rooms had always been out of reach. Sometimes in the spring, she had bought six tulips at a shop, unable to resist them, even though she knew Mellersh would think it was a waste of money if he found out. But they always died quickly, and that was that. As for the Judas tree, she didn't even know what it was; she just stared at it against the sky as if she were looking at a heavenly vision.

Mrs. Arbuthnot, coming out of her room, found her standing there in the middle of the hall, staring.
"Now what does she think she sees?"
Mrs. Wilkins said, turning to her with complete conviction.
said Mrs. Arbuthnot quickly, her smile fading.

Mrs. Arbuthnot had woken up with a wonderful sense of peace and relief, and she didn't want to hear that something was wrong. She hadn't even dreamed of Frederick. For the first time in years, she had been spared the recurring dream where he was with her and they were close, which always led to a sad awakening. She had slept like a baby and woken up feeling positive, finding that she only wanted to say
in her morning prayers. It was unsettling to suddenly be told that they were
—which usually sounded like a warning of trouble.

she asked anxiously.

Mrs. Wilkins looked at her for a moment and laughed.
asked Mrs. Arbuthnot, her face relaxing as Mrs. Wilkins laughed.

"We are. This place is. Everything. It's all so wonderful. It's funny and lovely that we're actually here. I bet that when we finally get to heaven—the one everyone talks about—it won't be any more beautiful than this."
Mrs. Arbuthnot smiled, feeling secure again.
"Have you ever been this happy in your entire life?"
Mrs. Wilkins asked, grabbing her arm.

Mrs. Arbuthnot said. And she never had been—not even during her early days of being in love with Frederick. Back then, pain had always been close by, bringing doubts and worries because she loved him so much. But this was a simple happiness of being in complete harmony with her surroundings. It was the kind of happiness that asks for nothing, but just enjoys the moment, breathes, and exists.
"Let's go take a closer look at that tree,"
"I can't believe it's just a tree."

Arm in arm, they walked down the hall, their faces looking so youthful and excited that their husbands wouldn't have recognized them. They stood together at the open window. After admiring the beautiful pink tree, their eyes wandered over the garden, and they saw Lady Caroline sitting on the low wall at the eastern edge, looking out over the bay with her feet resting among the lilies.

They were surprised. They stood completely still, arm in arm, staring down at her in silence.

She was also wearing a white dress, and her head was bare. Back in London, when her hat had been pulled down to her nose and her coat furs were up to her ears, they had no idea she was so pretty. They had simply thought she looked different from the other women at the club. The other members and the waitresses had noticed it too, glancing back at her as they walked past her corner. But they hadn't realized how stunning she was. She was extremely pretty, with very distinct features. Her blonde hair was very bright, her beautiful grey eyes were striking, her dark eyelashes were very dark, her skin was pale and clear, and her lips were very red. She was incredibly slender, but still had a graceful shape under her thin dress. She looked out across the bay, her silhouette clear against the blue sky. She sat in the bright sun, dangling her feet among the lilies as if she didn't care if they got bruised.
"She's going to get a headache sitting out in the sun like that,"
"Well, they belong to her as much as to us."

Lady Caroline turned her head. She looked up at them, surprised to see that they looked much younger and nicer than they had at the club. In fact, they were actually quite pleasant-looking, though they were wearing outdated clothes. Her eyes quickly sized them up in a fraction of a second before she smiled, waved, and called out,

She saw immediately that there was nothing interesting about their outfits. She wasn't thinking this consciously, as she was currently sick of high fashion and the effort it required. In her experience, as soon as you bought beautiful clothes, they took over your life, demanding to be worn to every social event. You didn't wear the clothes; the clothes wore you, dragging you out at all hours. No wonder men stayed young longer; a new pair of pants couldn't control their lives like that. Her thoughts were a bit random, but she liked to let her mind wander. As she got off the wall and walked toward the window, she felt relieved that she would be spending a month with people who wore simple, outdated dresses.
she said, looking up with a smile. She was truly charming, with perfect features and even a dimple.
"because we were planning to choose the best room for you."
"At least, I think it's the nicest one. It has windows on two sides—I love rooms like that, don't you? It looks west over the sea and north over this Judas tree."
"And we wanted to decorate it with flowers for you,"
"Oh, Domenico did that. I asked him to as soon as I arrived. He's the gardener, and he's wonderful."
"to be independent and know exactly what you want."
"Yes, it saves a lot of trouble,"
"But you shouldn't be so independent that you don't let others do nice things for you,"

Mrs. Wilkins said.

Lady Caroline, who had been looking at Mrs. Arbuthnot, now turned to Mrs. Wilkins. At the club in London, she had barely noticed Mrs. Wilkins because Mrs. Arbuthnot did all the talking. She had thought Mrs. Wilkins was too shy and awkward to converse with, remembering how she had struggled to say goodbye, blushing and looking uncomfortable. So she looked at her with surprise now, and was even more startled when Mrs. Wilkins looked at her with open admiration and said,
"I didn't realize you were so pretty."

She stared at Mrs. Wilkins. She wasn't used to people being so direct about her looks. Even though she was completely used to being admired—which was inevitable after twenty-eight years of it—she was surprised to hear it said so bluntly, especially by another woman.
"It's very nice of you to say so,"
Lady Caroline stared at Mrs. Arbuthnot.
"I make the most of it. I've been doing that for as long as I can remember."
Mrs. Arbuthnot said, smiling and shaking a warning finger,

Lady Caroline began to worry that these two women were eccentric characters. If so, she would be bored. Nothing annoyed her more than people who tried too hard to be unique and kept her talking. And the one who admired her—it would be annoying if she followed her around just to look at her. She wanted this holiday to be a complete escape from her normal life, a restful change. Being admired and followed around was just more of the same, not a contrast. Finding herself trapped with two eccentric people in a medieval castle on a steep hill—designed specifically to keep people in or out—didn't sound very relaxing. Maybe she should be a bit more distant. They had seemed so timid at the club, even the dark-haired one (whose name she couldn't remember), that she had thought it was safe to be friendly. But here, they had already come out of their shells. Neither of them seemed shy now. If they were this bold right away, they would soon start crowding her unless she set some boundaries. That would ruin her dream of thirty quiet, restful days, relaxing in the sun, recovering, and not being bothered, talked to, or hovered over by anyone. She just wanted to recover from the exhaustion of her hectic social life.

Besides, there was Mrs. Fisher. She had to keep her at a distance too. Lady Caroline had left two days early for two reasons: first, she wanted to arrive before the others to choose her favorite room, and second, she wanted to avoid traveling with Mrs. Fisher. She had no desire to travel or arrive with her, and saw no reason why she should have to spend any time with her at all.

Unfortunately, Mrs. Fisher had the exact same idea of arriving early to claim the best room, so she and Lady Caroline ended up traveling together anyway. They suspected it at Calais, feared it in Paris, knew it at Modane, and ignored it at Mezzago, taking two separate carriages to Castagneto, with one carriage driving right behind the other the entire way. But when the road ended at the church steps, they couldn't avoid each other anymore. Faced with this difficult final climb, they had no choice but to team up.

Because of Mrs. Fisher's walking stick, Lady Caroline had to handle everything. Mrs. Fisher explained from her carriage that she wanted to help, but her stick made it impossible. The drivers told Lady Caroline that they would need local boys to carry the luggage up to the castle, so she went to find some while Mrs. Fisher waited in the carriage. Mrs. Fisher could speak Italian, but only the classical Italian of Dante, which she had studied as a girl with the famous writer Matthew Arnold. She figured this would be too formal for the local boys, so Lady Caroline, who spoke normal Italian well, had to take charge.
Mrs. Fisher said, sitting firmly in her carriage.
"Please just think of me as an old woman with a walking stick."
And so, walking down the stone steps to the square, along the waterfront, and up the winding path, Lady Caroline was forced to walk as slowly with Mrs. Fisher as if she were her own grandmother.

Mrs. Fisher remarked calmly every now and then.

Whenever they rested on the benches along the path, Lady Caroline wanted to run ahead, but she had to stay with Mrs. Fisher to be polite. During these breaks, Mrs. Fisher told her about the time she walked up a similar path with the famous poet Tennyson.
Mrs. Fisher said, looking at her over her glasses.
"And it was a path very much like this one,"
"No eucalyptus trees, of course, but otherwise very similar. At one of the turns, he stopped and said to me—I can still picture him saying it—"

Yes, Mrs. Fisher would need to be kept at a distance. And so would the two women at the window. She should start setting boundaries right away. She regretted getting down from the wall; she should have just waved and waited for them to come down to the garden.

So she ignored Mrs. Arbuthnot's warning finger and said with attempted coldness that they probably wanted to get breakfast, and that she had already eaten. But unfortunately for her, no matter how coldly she spoke, her voice always sounded warm and pleasant. This was due to the natural shape of her throat and mouth, and had nothing to do with her actual mood. As a result, no one ever realized they were being snubbed. It was very annoying. Even when she tried to stare icily, it didn't work because her beautiful eyes were framed by long, soft, dark eyelashes. An icy look got lost in those lashes, making people think she was looking at them with deep, flattering interest. And whenever she was in a bad mood or angry, she just looked so sad and pathetic that everyone rushed to comfort her, usually by trying to hug or kiss her. It was absolutely maddening. Nature seemed determined to make her look and sound like an angel. She could never be rude without being completely misunderstood.
she said, trying her best to sound brief.
She nodded and walked back to sit on the wall, letting the cool lilies surround her feet again.
